what: National Fuel Gas is an unusual utility: it does four things along the same chain of gas. It drills for natural gas in Appalachia through Seneca Resources, gathers it, ships it through its own pipelines and storage fields, and sells it to households in western New York and Pennsylvania through a regulated distribution utility.
customers: Homeowners and businesses in its regulated service territory, plus pipeline shippers, gas marketers and utilities who buy the production and transport capacity.
money: Seneca Resources: natural gas wells in the Appalachian basin, sold at market prices.
Regulated transportation and seasonal storage, paid for by contracted capacity rather than volume.
Regulated gas distribution to roughly 750,000 customers in New York and Pennsylvania.
Gathering systems connecting its own wells to the pipeline network.
moat: Owning production, pipelines and the end customer means the company captures margin at each step and is less exposed to any single one. Its pipeline and storage assets have regulated returns, and building new interstate pipeline capacity in the Northeast is extremely difficult, which makes existing capacity more valuable.
risks: Natural gas prices drive the production segment, and revenue has swung widely: $3.1B in 2022 down to $1.9B in 2024 and back to $2.3B.
Free cash flow of $181.2M is far below net income of $665.4M, because drilling and pipeline spending absorb most of the cash.
Debt of $2.7B against only $43.2M of cash leaves little flexibility.
New York State's climate policy is hostile to natural gas distribution, which threatens the long-term growth of the utility segment.
Only two analysts cover the stock, so the $91.00 average target is a very thin consensus.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 10.4 times earnings and 6.3 times EV/EBITDA, cheap even for a utility.
Rising electricity demand from data centres increases demand for gas-fired generation in the Northeast, where pipeline capacity is scarce.
The regulated segments provide steady earnings that cushion the volatility of gas production.
The company has one of the longest dividend-increase records in the US utility sector.
watch: Whether free cash flow catches up with earnings. The business model is sound, but it currently consumes most of what it earns, so capital spending discipline is what would turn reported profit into shareholder returns.
